clue.text: Jumpy character who may surprise us and quit TV?

definitions.text: Jumpy character who may surprise us

parts.note: to jack in a job is to give it up
the box is informal for the television

explanation.surface: A twitchy person who might startle us and has walked out of a TV job.
explanation.walkthrough: To jack in is British slang for to quit, and the box is slang for television; read together they name a toy.
explanation.definitionFit: The toy is a spring-loaded figure that leaps out of its case when the lid opens, startling whoever opened it.

clue.text: What barmen sometimes add to whisky, right?

wordplay.words: What barmen sometimes add to whisky
wordplay.note: read as two words: nothing but frozen water, a common request with a spirit

explanation.surface: Asking whether a bartender's habit of adding something to a whisky is correct.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as 'just ice', it is what a bartender puts in a whisky on the rocks; the comma separates the definition, which is the noun right, not the yes-or-no word.
explanation.definitionFit: Justice and right are both nouns for fairness and what is morally due to someone.

clue.text: Plot emerging from Tory clubs two months before Christmas

parts.note: Con is short for Conservative, Britain's Tory party
C is the card-suit abbreviation for clubs
October comes two months before December; Oct is its calendar abbreviation

explanation.surface: A political scheme cooked up in Conservative clubs in late autumn.
explanation.definitionFit: To concoct a plan is to devise or hatch it, which is a verb sense of plot.

clue.text: Telling off about books obtained criminally

indicators.note: about means around, so these letters surround the others
off suggests something gone wrong or out of place, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: anagram fodder
OT is the Old Testament, a set of books of the Bible

explanation.surface: A scolding over some books that were stolen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Telling off' reads as a single phrase meaning a reprimand; here off is the instruction acting on the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Ill-gotten describes gains acquired dishonestly or by unlawful means.

clue.text: Levels of society mostly brought up making pastries

indicators.note: in a down entry, bringing something up means reading it from bottom to top
mostly means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: social strata are the layers of society

explanation.surface: The upper classes, by and large well raised, baking pastries.
explanation.definitionFit: Tarts are pastry cases with fillings, a kind of pastry.

clue.text: Head down, King sat for portrait that's unveiled

indicators.note: taking the head down removes the first letter

parts.note: Rex is Latin for king
a sitter poses for a painter

explanation.surface: With head bowed, the king sat for a portrait that has now been revealed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head down' looks like the king's posture; it means dropping the first letter of the Latin word for king.
explanation.definitionFit: Something exposed has been uncovered or revealed, just like something unveiled.

clue.text: Hoardings at intervals above a motorway displaying eastern art

indicators.note: at intervals means every other letter, skipping one each time

parts.note: second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters
taken as written
the M1 is Britain's main north-south motorway, written MI in crosswords

explanation.surface: Billboards spaced along a motorway showing Asian artwork.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'above' just places one piece before the next.
explanation.definitionFit: Origami is the Japanese craft of paper folding, an art from the Far East.

clue.text: Kevin maybe wrongly nagged over small breakfast dish

parts.note: Kevin Bacon is a Hollywood actor; maybe flags him as an example

indicators.note: wrongly means incorrectly arranged, so the letters must be put in a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder
S is the abbreviation for small

explanation.surface: Someone named Kevin unfairly scolded over a small breakfast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kevin maybe' looks like any Kevin; it is the actor, whose surname is the meat.
explanation.definitionFit: Bacon and eggs is the classic cooked breakfast plate, a fried morning meal.

clue.text: Ammunition factory aeroplane's radar captures heading west

indicators.note: in an across clue, going west means reading right to left
the words grip the letters inside them, so the run is held within the phrase

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the first word into the start of the second

explanation.surface: An aircraft's radar picks up a munitions works as it flies west.
explanation.definitionFit: An arsenal is a place where weapons and ammunition are made or stored.

clue.text: Salesperson is economical with the truth giving answers

parts.note: a rep is a sales representative
a polite phrase for telling untruths

explanation.surface: A sales rep dodges the truth while answering questions.
explanation.definitionFit: Replies and answers are synonymous plural nouns for responses given to questions.

clue.text: Resolute individual, disliked

parts.note: single means one, individual
to mind something is to object to it

explanation.surface: A determined person whom nobody likes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Individual' looks like a noun for a person; it is the adjective meaning one.
explanation.definitionFit: Single-minded means fixed on one purpose, determined and unwavering, as resolute is.

clue.text: Foreign banker's gold company keeps in Tokyo ultimately

indicators.note: something that keeps another thing holds it inside

parts.note: or is gold in heraldry
taken as written

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of the word before it

parts.note: last letter of Tokyo
standard abbreviation for company

explanation.surface: A foreign bank's gold reserves are held by a firm in Tokyo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Banker' looks like a financier, but in crosswords it is something with banks: a river. Gold and company together surround the inner pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The Orinoco is a great South American river flowing through Venezuela, and a river has banks.

clue.text: American retreats when facing black bear

indicators.note: retreating means going backwards, so the word is read from the end

parts.note: standard abbreviation for American
to black something is to blacken or stain it

explanation.surface: An American backs away on coming face to face with a black bear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Black bear' reads as one animal, but black is a verb for the wordplay and bear is the definition, a verb too.
explanation.definitionFit: To sustain a weight or a loss is to bear or endure it.

clue.text: Core of idea entertained by suitable expert

indicators.note: a guest entertained by a host is inside their house

parts.note: apt means fitting or suitable

indicators.note: the core of a word is its central letters, with the outer ones stripped off

parts.note: middle two letters of idea

explanation.surface: The central point of a notion is welcomed by a fitting specialist.
explanation.definitionFit: An adept is a noun for a highly skilled person, a master of some craft.

clue.text: Exercise equipment doctor trialled, Mike admitted

indicators.note: someone admitted is let inside, so this letter goes within the others
to doctor something is to tamper with it, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder
Mike is M in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A gym machine that a doctor tested, with someone called Mike let in.
explanation.definitionFit: A treadmill is a running machine with a moving belt, a staple of gyms.

clue.text: Raising tax popular? At heart Green member claims that

indicators.note: a member that claims something takes hold of it, so those letters go inside
the heart of a word is its central letter

parts.note: middle letter of green
a leg is a limb, a member of the body
VAT is value added tax, the UK sales tax
in means fashionable, popular

explanation.surface: Is a tax rise popular? At its core, a Green Party member says so.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member' suggests a party member next to Green, but it is a limb; the Green supplies only its centre.
explanation.definitionFit: Elevating means lifting something higher, the same verb sense as raising.

clue.text: Command Macedonian criminal to leave area

indicators.note: criminal suggests something crooked, so the letters are twisted out of order
something told to leave departs, so that letter is dropped

parts.note: anagram fodder
standard abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: An order telling a Macedonian lawbreaker to get out of the district.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Command' looks like a verb giving an order, but it is a noun meaning control.
explanation.definitionFit: Command as a noun means authority or control over others, which is what dominance is.

clue.text: Flipping fabrics I order getting wet

indicators.note: flipping something turns it over, so the sequence is read from the end

parts.note: net is a mesh fabric
taken as written
OM is the Order of Merit, a British honour

explanation.surface: Exasperated by the cloth I ordered, I end up soaked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' looks like a mild British swear word; it is the turnaround signal. OM is the Order of Merit.
explanation.definitionFit: To moisten something is to make it slightly damp, so it is a verb meaning to wet.

clue.text: Record song after summit of nations for planet

indicators.note: after places these pieces following the first letter in the entry
the summit is the top, and in a down entry the top letter is the first

parts.note: first letter of nations
an EP is an extended-play record
a tune is a melody or song

explanation.surface: Recording a song after a world summit, in honour of a planet.
explanation.definitionFit: Neptune is the eighth and outermost planet of the solar system, named after the Roman sea god.

clue.text: Saw team back from physio in morning

indicators.note: these pieces sit inside the outer phrase

parts.note: am is the abbreviation for morning

indicators.note: the back of a word is its final letter

parts.note: last letter of physio
a cricket or football team is an eleven, XI in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Seeing a squad return from physiotherapy early in the day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw' looks like the past tense of see, but it is a noun for an old saying.
explanation.definitionFit: A saw is a traditional maxim, and an axiom is likewise an accepted truth or principle.

clue.text: Essay, article on European politician tense Times defends

indicators.note: to defend something is to surround and shield it

parts.note: a is the indefinite article
T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense
T stands for time, so times doubles it
standard abbreviation for European
an MP is a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A newspaper essay about a nervous European politician that the Times stands up for.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Essay' looks like a piece of writing; as a verb or noun it also means a try. In a down clue 'on' puts the article above the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: An essay in its older sense is a try or effort, so it is a synonym of attempt.

clue.text: More bananas with meal daughter put away holding appeal

indicators.note: holding means grasping something inside
putting something away removes it from view, so that letter goes

parts.note: dinner is a main meal
D is the genealogical abbreviation for daughter
SA is sex appeal

explanation.surface: Extra bananas served with a meal that a daughter ate up, with some charm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bananas' looks like fruit next to a meal, but it is slang for crazy; 'put away' could mean eaten, but it removes a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Bananas is informal for mad, so more bananas is the comparative, crazier.

clue.text: Hugged premier of Greece, extremely drunk

indicators.note: premier means first, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: first letter of Greece
ripped is slang for very intoxicated

explanation.surface: Greece's prime minister, very drunk, embraced someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Premier' suggests a head of government, but it only asks for a first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To grip someone is to hold them tightly, as in a hug or clasp.

clue.text: Sketch from current broadcast

indicators.note: something broadcast is heard over the airwaves, so we go by sound rather than spelling

parts.note: a draught is a current of air

explanation.surface: A comedy sketch taken from a current-affairs programme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' looks like topical news; it is a flow of air, spelt the British way.
explanation.definitionFit: A draft is a preliminary drawing or outline, which is what a sketch is.

clue.text: Engineer trains a skilled worker

indicators.note: to engineer something is to construct it, building these letters into a new word

parts.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: An engineer coaches a skilled tradesperson.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Engineer' reads as a noun doing the training; it is a verb telling you to rebuild the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An artisan is a craftsperson working with their hands at a skilled trade.

clue.text: Fruit from Asia, it is cut regularly by mum

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is taken

parts.note: second, fourth, sixth letters and so on
ma is an informal name for one's mother

explanation.surface: A fruit imported from Asia is sliced neatly by Mum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' looks like the action of slicing, but it belongs to the letters being sampled.
explanation.definitionFit: A satsuma is a small, loose-skinned citrus fruit like a mandarin, originally from Japan.

clue.text: This writer's pieces essentially used to be great

parts.note: the setter refers to themselves: I am, contracted
chessmen are pieces

indicators.note: the essence of a word is its centre, so the middle letters are taken

parts.note: middle two letters of used

explanation.surface: A writer reflects that their works were basically used to being great.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Used to be' reads as a past-tense phrase; used supplies letters and 'to be' just joins the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Great in the sense of very large in size matches immense, meaning huge.

clue.text: Detective to visit suspect with anger

indicators.note: suspect as an adjective means dubious or unreliable, so the letters are not in their trustworthy order

parts.note: anagram fodder
anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A detective goes to call on a suspect in a rage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suspect' looks like the noun, a person under suspicion, but it is the adjective signalling rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: An investigator is someone who looks into crimes, such as a police or private detective.
